reviews.name: Mubasheer Nawaz Mohammed
reviews.text:
A Sanctuary of True Brotherhood: Islamic Center of Parsippany.

Walking into our local masjid, which opened its doors just two years ago, feels less like entering a place of worship and more like coming home. In an era where community spaces can sometimes feel rigid, this masjid stands as a glowing testament to the true Islamic values of **hospitality, equality, and open-heartedness.**

** The Spirit of Welcome**
The management deserves immense credit for the atmosphere they have cultivated. From day one, they have treated every congregant not just as a visitor, but as a stakeholder. Their "brotherly" approach isn't just a polite gesture; it’s a lived philosophy. They go out of their way to ensure that everyone—regardless of background, age, or status—feels that this is our masjid. Brother Shafi with his ever smiling and welcoming face greets everyone alike and treats you as his own extended family.

One of the most beautiful aspects of this community is the total absence of discrimination. In every row of prayer, you see a mosaic of cultures and stories, all treated with the same profound respect. There is a rare, refreshing sincerity here; no one is a stranger for more than a few minutes.

The masjid’s commitment to accessibility is truly remarkable, Unlike many places that close after Isha, this masjid remains open **24/7**.

It serves as a sanctuary for prayer, a quiet corner for reflection, and a hub for daily activities.

Whether it’s the early hours of Tahajjud or the height of Jumu'ah, the welcoming energy never wavers.

This isn't just a masjid built of bricks and mortar; it is a community built on **genuine love and inclusion.** If you are looking for a place to ground your soul and find a brotherhood that embraces you exactly as you are, you will find it here.

"It’s more than a masjid; it’s a reminder of what a community should feel like."

May Allah bring a lot of barakah in brother Shafi’s livelihood and bless his family, Ameen.

reviews.text:
Unfortunately, my experience at this mosque was very disappointing, especially as a parent. I brought my 3-year-old son to Friday prayer for the first time, hoping to introduce him to the mosque, prayer, and our Islamic traditions.

He was not running around or being loud. We were simply speaking very quietly while I explained to him what was happening. Despite this, we were warned three times and eventually asked to leave the mosque.

I believe mosques should be welcoming places where young children can gradually learn about Islam and develop a love for the masjid. Making a 3-year-old and his father feel unwelcome over quiet conversation does not reflect the patience and compassion we should show toward children in Islam.

Unfortunately, I would not consider this mosque child- or family-friendly based on our experience.

reviews.text:
PLEASE READ THIS...
I came to El Zahra Islamic Center for the first time during one of the most difficult moments of my life.

My parents were both Muslim. I lost my father three years ago, and just two months ago, I lost my mother. When I walked into El Zahra, I was carrying grief, uncertainty, and a tremendous responsibility. I needed guidance and support as I navigated my mother's funeral and services. I had done things differently at other points in my life and within my culture, and more than anything, I wanted to make sure I was honoring my mother and the faith she believed in—that she would be at peace, that she would be received with mercy, and that she would have the opportunity to rise again as she believed.

I will be completely honest: I was prepared for something very different.

I expected strictness. I expected rigidity. I expected to be questioned or made to feel that I didn't know enough or wasn't doing things the "right" way. I couldn't have been more wrong.

From the moment I walked through the doors, I was met with kindness, patience, compassion, and understanding. The Sheikh spoke to me with warmth and never once made me feel judged. No one questioned my background, my choices, or where I was in my journey. They simply helped me.

And that meant more to me than I can possibly express.

I am a Palestinian American, and while that is an important part of who I am, I want to be very clear that my experience at El Zahra was not about race, ethnicity, or culture. It was about humanity. I saw people of different backgrounds, races, and walks of life welcomed with the same kindness and dignity.

For the first time in a very long time, I didn't feel like an outsider trying to figure out where I belonged. I felt like I was around family—and at that particular moment in my life, I desperately needed family.

El Zahra gave me something I didn't know I needed: reassurance that faith can be welcoming rather than intimidating, compassionate rather than judgmental, and deeply human.

I will forever be grateful to the Sheikh and everyone at El Zahra Islamic Center for the support, guidance, and compassion they showed me during the loss of my mother.

Sometimes a place of worship is more than a building.

Sometimes, when you are hurting, it becomes the place where someone helps you find your way home.

Thank you, El Zahra, for being that place for me.

reviews.text:
I had a deeply disappointing experience at this mosque. A mosque should be a place where people can worship peacefully, with dignity and respect. Unfortunately, during my visit, people were playing soccer inside the prayer area while others were trying to pray.

While I was performing my prayer, I was hit by the ball twice—once in the chest and once in the arm. This was more than a minor distraction. I could not focus on my prayer without worrying about being hit again. No one should have to deal with that in a place of worship.

What upset me most was the lack of consideration for the people who had come to pray. I understand that a mosque is also a gathering place for families and the community, and I welcome that. But playing soccer in the same space where people are actively praying crosses a clear line. Recreational activities need an appropriate space and time so they do not interfere with worship.

I hope the mosque’s leadership takes this concern seriously and establishes clear rules to protect the prayer area. People should be able to come here knowing they can pray without balls flying toward them or games taking place around them.

Based on this experience, I do not plan to return with my family. It is upsetting to say that about a mosque, but the atmosphere during my visit was far from the peace and respect I expected. Wallahul-Mustaan .
